analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue pesticide manufacturers for damages when pesticides injure them or their property.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill has sat untouched in the Senate Agriculture Committee ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal pesticide law currently offers no route for an individual to sue the manufacturer of a pesticide that hurt them or damaged their property; courts have generally read the law as blocking those suits. This bill writes a new section into that law creating a direct right to sue a pesticide's registered manufacturer in federal court for compensatory and punitive damages, while leaving state-law claims untouched. It was referred to the Agriculture Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People physically injured by pesticides and owners of property damaged by them — farmworkers and households near sprayed fields being the most exposed groups — gain a federal courtroom route to compensation, including punitive damages, against the company that registered the pesticide.

how_it_helps.text: Any person whose person or property is injured by a pesticide may sue the pesticide's registrant in federal district court for monetary damages [S2].
Recoverable damages include compensatory and punitive damages at the court's discretion [S2].
The new federal claim does not preempt state-law claims, so injured people could pursue both avenues [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers that register products with the EPA would face new damage liability, including punitive damages, for injuries their products cause, and those costs would eventually show up in prices and insurance for farm operations.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars recovery of attorney's fees and court costs, so injured people must front their own litigation costs, which can make suits uneconomic for the very workers most likely to be harmed [S2].

Manufacturers and some courts argue the EPA already vets pesticide labels and that letting juries second-guess registered, lawfully used products through punitive-damage suits raises costs and litigation risk across agriculture — a cost that can pass through to food prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it gives injured people a path to compensation where current federal law effectively leaves them with none, and it does not displace stronger state claims. The honest tradeoff is that liability for lawful, EPA-approved products carries cost and uncertainty, and the no-attorney's-fees design shifts litigation expenses onto injured plaintiffs rather than defendants.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on July 17, 2025, and nothing has happened since [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the bill on July 17, 2025 [S1][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S4].
No further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote has occurred; the Congress is still in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, pesticide manufacturers, since the liability the bill would create has not advanced toward law.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee [S1][S4].

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 17, 2025 and has taken no action on it since [S4].

against.name: Sen. John Boozman
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, has not scheduled any consideration of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats are attached to the bill — one sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no votes have occurred, so no partisan split on the merits is on the record [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill creates federal court liability, including punitive damages, for injuries caused by their products — an exposure current federal law largely does not provide. Today the cost of pesticide injuries falls on exposed workers and neighbors; the bill would shift a share of it back to the makers.
Liability runs against registrants, not farmers, but higher manufacturer costs could pass through to pesticide prices and farm budgets.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no committee action four-plus months after referral, and the Agriculture Committee not scheduling it, the realistic path is that the bill dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless it picks up substantial new support.
